patent: Filed 1987-09-17 and issued 1990-01-16 to Arthur Ashkin and Joseph M. Dziedzic of AT&T Bell Laboratories. It claims the single-beam gradient force optical trap, now called optical tweezers, driven by an infrared laser (claim 1: 0.8 to 1.8 µm) so that cells, bacteria and other biological particles are held and moved without optical damage, with the trapping objective also used for viewing, and a second trap formed through the same objective (claims 4-5). The trap itself had been shown on dielectric particles with 514.5 nm light (Ashkin, Dziedzic, Bjorkholm and Chu, Optics Letters 1986, vol. 11, p.288), and Ashkin and Dziedzic had trapped viruses and bacteria with visible light (Science 1987, vol. 235, p.1517). The infrared work appeared as Ashkin, Dziedzic and Yamane, "Optical trapping and manipulation of single cells using infrared laser beams", Nature 1987, vol. 330, p.769. Ashkin shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics, cited for the optical tweezers and their application to biological systems.

figs.1: Trapping path, top to bottom: IR laser 10, diverging lens 12 on x-y-z mount 13, expanded beam 14 filling the hatched objective 23, which focuses through immersion liquid 24 into cell 25; the rays cross at trapped particle 27. Under the cell, on stage mount 26, converging lens 28 sends light from source 29 up through the cell into the same objective. Of the two diagonal plates, the lower one, 19, reflects visible light to eyepiece 21 (filter 22, eye at right); the upper one, 15, reflects what passes 19 to monitor 18 (filter 17). The dash-dot horizontal lines are these viewing paths.
figs.2: FIG. 1 with a second trapping beam added at upper right: IR laser 30, beam 31, diverging lens 32 on mount 33, and beam 34 (solid rays) reflected by plate 35 into the same objective, while the first beam (dashed rays) passes through 35. In the cell two ray crossings appear: the central one is the first trap, the one to its right holds particle 36. Unlabelled elements are those of FIG. 1.
figs.3: Enlarged cell with the beam entering from above (objective not drawn). Dash-dot lines are the edges of the converging and then diverging beam; the curved lines draw the beam narrowing to its waist in mid-liquid, where one particle is held. Short dashes are the liquid, left blank inside the beam cone.
figs.4: Same cell with the focus moved down onto the inner surface of the bottom plate. A small cluster of particles sits in the waist on the plate: the plate stops them along the beam axis and the gradient holds them sideways.
figs.5: Focus moved below the cell: the beam is still converging where it crosses the bottom plate, and the waist (curved lines) lies outside the cell. Many particles spread across the wider beam on the plate, held sideways by the inward-pointing scattering force of the converging rays and stopped axially by the plate.

parts.22: The text calls 22 both "eyepiece 22" and "Infrared blocking filter 22"; the drawing shows 22 as a plate between eyepiece 21 and the eye, matching the filter.
parts.35: The text gives two forms: a mirror that reflects beam 34 and transmits beam 14 because the two lasers run at different wavelengths, or a beam splitter that reflects about half of the incident light and transmits the rest.
parts.26: Moves the cell in x, y and z; the text uses it to locate, translate, separate and isolate trapped particles.

glossary.def: A single, tightly focused laser beam that holds a small particle near the focus. Now called optical tweezers.
The force on a polarizable particle toward higher light intensity, proportional to the intensity gradient; in a focused beam it points toward the focus.
Radiation pressure from light scattered or absorbed by the particle, pushing it along the direction the light travels.
Refractive index of the medium times the sine of the half-angle of the light cone a lens collects or delivers; a higher value gives a tighter focus. Values above 1 require an immersion liquid.
A microscope objective used with water or oil filling the gap to the sample, so the light cone is not limited by refraction at an air gap.
A partially reflecting plate or cube that sends part of a beam one way and the rest another; a dichroic version splits by wavelength.
A filter that passes visible light and absorbs or reflects infrared, here keeping back-reflected trapping light from the eye and the camera monitor.

Particles much larger than the wavelength (Mie, treated with ray optics) versus much smaller (Rayleigh, treated as a point dipole); the direction of the trapping force depends on shape only in the Mie case.
The ability of a cell or organism to move by itself, used here as a sign the trapped particle was not damaged.
A rod-shaped plant virus, the first virus to be identified.
The lens below the sample that concentrates illumination onto it; converging lens 28 plays this role.
